title: Oracle Identity Column: Examples, Options and ORA-00001 Fix
description: Create an Oracle identity column with GENERATED ALWAYS or BY DEFAULT ON NULL, get the new ID in PL/SQL, and fix ORA-00001 with START WITH LIMIT VALUE.

sources.title: Oracle 19c SQL Reference: ALTER TABLE (identity_options, START WITH LIMIT VALUE, DROP IDENTITY)

reviewNotes: All examples written from the Oracle 19c SQL Reference and not executed; please test-run on 19c and 23ai. Check: (1) the RETURNING INTO output 'New order id: 4' assumes the failed ORA-32795/32796 statements did not consume sequence values; adjust if they do. (2) The ALWAYS-with-explicit-NULL cell in the comparison table (ORA-32795) and the BY DEFAULT explicit-NULL ORA-01400 message format. (3) That 'MODIFY ... GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY (START WITH LIMIT VALUE)' keeps the column usable as shown, and the docs' note that other options revert to defaults when START WITH changes (does omitting ON NULL drop it?). (4) The ORA-00001 message is shown in 19c format; 23ai prints table and column names too. (5) ISEQ$$_ numbers in the dictionary output are placeholders. (6) TRUNCATE not resetting the identity and the hot-index-block note are general Oracle behaviour, not from a specific doc page. The ISEQ$$ naming is not stated on docs.oracle.com; it is widely observed.

data.text: An Oracle identity column is a numeric column that fills itself with the next number every time you insert a row. You declare it with GENERATED AS IDENTITY in CREATE TABLE, and Oracle creates and manages a sequence for it behind the scenes. It is Oracle's built-in answer to AUTO_INCREMENT in MySQL and has been available since Oracle Database 12c Release 1.

There are three variants: GENERATED ALWAYS, GENERATED BY DEFAULT and GENERATED BY DEFAULT ON NULL. They differ in one thing: whether you are allowed to supply your own value. This tutorial shows each one on a small table, the errors each one raises, how to get the new ID back in PL/SQL, and how to fix the most common production problem: ORA-00001 after someone loads rows with their own IDs.
How an identity column works

When you create an identity column, Oracle creates a system-generated sequence and links it to the column. On every INSERT that needs a value, Oracle takes the next number from that sequence. You never create, name or drop this sequence yourself. Its name looks like ISEQ$$_74321, and the number differs on every database.
Oracle also adds a NOT NULL constraint to the column automatically. It does not add a primary key or unique constraint. If the column is your key, declare PRIMARY KEY yourself.
The three generation types behave like this:
If you write just GENERATED AS IDENTITY with no keyword, you get ALWAYS. That is the safest choice for a surrogate key, because no application code can put its own number in the column.
A few rules from the Oracle documentation apply to every variant:

items.content: Only one identity column per table.
The data type must be numeric, usually NUMBER. You cannot use a user-defined type.
You cannot combine the identity clause with a DEFAULT clause on the same column.
CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT copies the values but not the identity property.

data.text: Sample setup
Run this in any schema where you can create tables. The orders table uses GENERATED ALWAYS, the usual choice for a key that only the database should assign.

data.caption: Sample table with a GENERATED ALWAYS identity column

data.text: None of the INSERT statements mention order_id. Oracle fills it in:

data.caption: Check the generated IDs

data.text: Output (expected output). The sequence starts at 1 and goes up by 1, because those are the defaults when you give no identity options.
GENERATED ALWAYS: Oracle owns the value
Step 1: try to insert your own ID
With ALWAYS, any attempt to supply a value is rejected, even a NULL:

data.code:
INSERT INTO orders (order_id, customer_name, amount)
VALUES (10, 'Vikram', 500);
data.caption: Explicit value into an ALWAYS column

data.code: ORA-32795: cannot insert into a generated always identity column
data.caption: Output (expected output)

data.text: Step 2: try to update the ID

data.caption: Updating an ALWAYS column

data.code: ORA-32796: cannot update a generated always identity column
data.caption: Output (expected output)

data.text: This is the point of ALWAYS. The key cannot be changed by mistake, and it cannot collide with numbers that some script invented. The cost is that data migrations which must keep the old IDs need an extra step, covered later in this article.
GENERATED BY DEFAULT and BY DEFAULT ON NULL
Use BY DEFAULT when you sometimes need to supply the ID yourself, for example when copying rows from another system and keeping their original numbers.

data.caption: BY DEFAULT accepts an explicit value

data.text: Output (expected output). The first row got a generated value. The second row kept the 500 you supplied. Supplying a value does not move the sequence, so the next generated value is still 2.
The NULL trap

Many applications and ORMs send every column in the INSERT, including the key, with NULL when they have no value. Plain BY DEFAULT treats that NULL as your explicit value, and the implicit NOT NULL constraint rejects it:

data.code:
INSERT INTO payments (payment_id, order_id, amount)
VALUES (NULL, 3, 4300.00);
data.caption: Explicit NULL into a BY DEFAULT column

data.code: ORA-01400: cannot insert NULL into ("APP"."PAYMENTS"."PAYMENT_ID")
data.caption: Output (expected output, schema name will be yours)

data.text: ON NULL fixes this. With GENERATED BY DEFAULT ON NULL AS IDENTITY, Oracle generates a value whenever the INSERT would store NULL, whether you left the column out or passed NULL on purpose:

data.caption: BY DEFAULT ON NULL generates a value for NULL

data.text: Output (expected output). Both rows got generated IDs. ON NULL only applies to INSERT. An UPDATE that sets the column to NULL still fails, because the column is NOT NULL.

data.title: Which one should you pick?
data.text: Use ALWAYS for new tables where only Oracle should assign keys. Use BY DEFAULT ON NULL when a framework sends NULL for the key, or when you must load rows with existing IDs. Plain BY DEFAULT without ON NULL is rarely what you want.
Set the start value, step and cache
The identity options take the same parameters as CREATE SEQUENCE. Put them in brackets after the identity clause:

data.caption: Identity options in brackets

data.text: Output (expected output). CACHE 100 makes Oracle keep 100 values ready in memory instead of the default 20. Oracle's own CREATE TABLE documentation recommends a CACHE higher than 20 for identity columns to improve performance. The trade-off is covered in the performance section below.
Get the generated ID back in PL/SQL

After inserting an order you usually need its new ID, for example to insert the order lines. Do not run SELECT MAX(order_id) for this. Another session may insert a row between your INSERT and your SELECT. Use the RETURNING INTO clause, which hands back the value from your own INSERT:

data.caption: RETURNING INTO gives you the new identity value

data.code: New order id: 4
data.caption: Output (expected output, with SET SERVEROUTPUT ON)

data.text: The 4 assumes the failed statements earlier did not use up sequence values. If your number is higher, that is normal. Identity values can have gaps, and your code should never depend on them being consecutive.
Find the sequence behind an identity column

The USER_TAB_IDENTITY_COLS view lists every identity column in your schema with its generation type and the name of its sequence. Use ALL_TAB_IDENTITY_COLS or DBA_TAB_IDENTITY_COLS to see other schemas.

data.caption: List identity columns and their sequences

data.text: Output (expected output, the ISEQ$$ numbers will differ). GENERATION_TYPE shows only ALWAYS or BY DEFAULT. The IDENTITY_OPTIONS column in the same view shows the start value, increment, cache and other settings as text.

data.title: Do not drop the ISEQ$$ sequence
data.text: DROP SEQUENCE ISEQ$$_74321 fails with ORA-32794: cannot drop a system-generated sequence. To remove the identity behaviour, use ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY ... DROP IDENTITY instead.
Fix ORA-00001 after loading rows with your own IDs

This is the problem that brings most people to identity columns in a hurry. Someone loads rows into a BY DEFAULT column with their own IDs. The sequence does not know about those rows. Later, the sequence reaches one of those numbers and the INSERT fails.
Step 1: reproduce the problem

data.caption: Explicit IDs run ahead of the sequence

data.code: ORA-00001: unique constraint (APP.PAYMENTS_PK) violated
data.caption: Output (expected output, 19c format)

data.text: Newer releases add the table and column names to the ORA-00001 message, but the cause is the same. The sequence is behind the data.
Step 2: move the sequence past the highest value

START WITH LIMIT VALUE exists only for identity columns and only in ALTER TABLE MODIFY. Oracle locks the table, finds the highest value in the column, and makes the next generated value that maximum plus the increment.

data.code:
ALTER TABLE payments MODIFY payment_id
  GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY (START WITH LIMIT VALUE);
data.caption: Reset the identity to MAX + increment
Insert again
Output (expected output)

data.text: The highest value was 500, so the new row got 501. Notice that this also skips over the free numbers 4 to 499. That is fine for a surrogate key, which only needs to be unique.

data.title: Restate every option when you change START WITH
data.text: The ALTER TABLE documentation says that if you change START WITH, all other identity options go back to their defaults unless you list them. If the column had CACHE 100 or ON NULL, include them again in the same statement, for example GENERATED BY DEFAULT ON NULL AS IDENTITY (START WITH LIMIT VALUE CACHE 100). Check USER_TAB_IDENTITY_COLS afterwards.
Change or remove an identity column
Switch ALWAYS to BY DEFAULT for a data load
To load rows with fixed IDs into an ALWAYS table, switch it to BY DEFAULT, load, move the sequence past the data, and switch back:

data.caption: Temporarily allow explicit IDs

data.text: Remove the identity property

data.code: ALTER TABLE orders MODIFY order_id DROP IDENTITY;
data.caption: Turn the column back into a plain NUMBER

data.text: This removes the sequence and the implicit NOT NULL constraint. Existing values stay as they are. The primary key you declared yourself stays too.
You cannot convert an existing column
You cannot turn an existing plain column into an identity column with ALTER TABLE MODIFY:

data.caption: Trying to convert an existing column

data.code: ORA-30673: column to be modified is not an identity column
data.caption: Output (expected output)

data.text: The usual options are to keep the column and fill it from a normal sequence with DEFAULT customer_seq.NEXTVAL, or to add a new identity column with ALTER TABLE ... ADD. When you add a new identity column, Oracle fills all existing rows from the sequence, but the documentation says the order in which rows get their numbers is not deterministic.
Identity column vs sequence vs trigger
Before 12c, the usual way to auto-number a key was a sequence plus a BEFORE INSERT trigger. You still see this in older code. Here is how the options compare:

content: Copied by CREATE TABLE AS SELECT

data.text: For a new table that just needs a unique key, use an identity column. Use your own sequence when several tables must share one number range, or when you need to fetch the next number before the INSERT. Avoid the trigger approach in new code. It adds a PL/SQL call for every row and does nothing an identity column cannot do.
Common mistakes

items.content: Assuming the identity column is the primary key. Oracle adds only NOT NULL. Without your own PRIMARY KEY or UNIQUE constraint, explicit values in a BY DEFAULT column can create duplicates.
Using plain BY DEFAULT with a framework that sends NULL. You get ORA-01400. Use BY DEFAULT ON NULL.
Loading data with explicit IDs and forgetting the sequence. Everything works until the sequence catches up, then you get ORA-00001. Run START WITH LIMIT VALUE after every such load.
Expecting TRUNCATE to restart numbering. TRUNCATE removes rows. It does not reset the sequence. To restart, use ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY ... (START WITH 1) on the empty table.
Reading the new ID with MAX(). It is wrong when other sessions insert at the same time. Use RETURNING INTO.

Expecting no gaps. Rolled-back inserts, failed statements and cached values lost at instance shutdown or failure all leave gaps. Never use an identity column where the business needs consecutive numbers, such as some invoice numbering rules.
Copying a table with CREATE TABLE AS SELECT and expecting auto-numbering. The copy has a plain NUMBER column. Create the new table with the identity clause first, then copy the rows into it.

data.text: Performance tips

items.content: Raise CACHE on busy tables. Each time the cache runs out, Oracle updates the sequence in the data dictionary. With a larger cache this happens less often. Oracle recommends a value above the default of 20 for identity columns.
Accept the gaps that cache causes. If the instance fails or shuts down abnormally, unused cached values are lost. With CACHE 100 you can lose up to 100 numbers. That is harmless for a surrogate key.

Leave NOORDER in place. NOORDER is the default. The CREATE SEQUENCE documentation notes that guaranteed order is usually not important for primary keys, and in Oracle RAC, ORDER adds coordination between instances.

Know the hot index block. Increasing keys from many sessions all insert into the right-hand edge of the primary key index. On very high insert rates this can become a point of contention. Measure before you change anything, for example with AWR wait events.

data.text: Frequently asked questions
Does Oracle have auto increment?
Yes. Since Oracle 12c, an identity column (GENERATED AS IDENTITY) is Oracle's auto increment. In 11g and earlier there is no such clause, and you use a sequence with a BEFORE INSERT trigger.
How do I reset an identity column in Oracle?

Use ALTER TABLE MODIFY with a new START WITH. (START WITH LIMIT VALUE) continues after the current highest value. (START WITH 1) restarts from 1, which you should only do on an empty table or you will get ORA-00001.
What is the difference between an identity column and a sequence in Oracle?

An identity column uses a sequence internally, but Oracle creates and owns it, it belongs to one column of one table, and with ALWAYS it blocks manual values. A standalone sequence is an object you manage and can use from any table or PL/SQL code.
Can I insert a value into an identity column in Oracle?
Only if it is GENERATED BY DEFAULT or BY DEFAULT ON NULL. With GENERATED ALWAYS you get ORA-32795. If you insert your own values, move the sequence afterwards with START WITH LIMIT VALUE.
Can I make an existing column an identity column?
No. ALTER TABLE MODIFY on a non-identity column raises ORA-30673. Add a new identity column, or use a column default of sequence.NEXTVAL on the existing column.
Summary

items.content: Use GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY for new surrogate keys; Oracle blocks manual values.
Use GENERATED BY DEFAULT ON NULL when tools send NULL or you must load existing IDs.
Declare PRIMARY KEY yourself; the identity clause only adds NOT NULL.
Get the new ID with RETURNING INTO, never with MAX().
After loading explicit IDs, run START WITH LIMIT VALUE and restate CACHE and ON NULL.
Find the hidden sequence in USER_TAB_IDENTITY_COLS; never try to drop it.
Raise CACHE on busy tables and treat gaps as normal.

linkedin.post:
Your insert fails with ORA-00001 on a table where Oracle generates the ID. The sequence is behind the data.

Oracle identity columns in 5 points:

→ GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY: only Oracle sets the value. Manual values raise ORA-32795.
→ GENERATED BY DEFAULT ON NULL: you may supply an ID, and NULL still gets a generated one. Plain BY DEFAULT rejects NULL with ORA-01400.
→ The identity clause adds NOT NULL, not a primary key. Declare PRIMARY KEY yourself.
→ Need the new ID in PL/SQL? Use RETURNING order_id INTO v_order_id, never SELECT MAX().
→ Loaded rows with your own IDs? Run ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY ... (START WITH LIMIT VALUE). Oracle moves the sequence past the highest value.

One trap: changing START WITH resets the other options, so restate CACHE and ON NULL in the same statement.

Do your new tables use identity columns, or are you still writing sequence plus trigger?
